title: Metadata Formats (Technical)
subheading: A technical guide to how audio tags are stored in each format.

contents.Text: [[[strong:Just want to know which format to choose?]]] The [[[button:Codecs][/_Guides/Codecs]]] guide explains it simply, without the technical breakdown.

Metadata is the information stored inside an audio file, such as the title, artist, album, genre, track number and cover art. It is what lets a player display and sort your music properly, without relying on file names.
•[[[strong:Same fields, different names:]]] Every format stores the title, artist, album and so on, but each uses its own names and structure. See [[[strong:Common fields compared]]] below.
•[[[strong:Converting:]]] Common fields normally carry over, but [[[strong:custom fields]]] and unusual frames may be lost.
•[[[strong:Simplest:]]] [[[strong:Vorbis comments]]] use plain KEY=value text, with any custom key and multiple values.
•[[[strong:Non-English text:]]] Safest in [[[strong:Vorbis comments]]], [[[strong:MP4 tags]]] and [[[strong:ID3v2.4]]], which all use UTF-8. [[[strong:WAV]]] has the weakest support.
[[[italics:Frame based]]] - Used by MP3 files.
Each piece of information is stored in its own frame, identified by a four-character ID. An ID3v2 tag sits at the start of the file and can hold Unicode text, lyrics and embedded images.

•[[[strong:ID3v2.3]]] - The most widely compatible version. Text is stored as ISO-8859-1 or UTF-16, and each frame holds a single value, so multiple artists have to be joined into one string with a separator.
•[[[strong:ID3v2.4]]] - The newest version. It adds UTF-8 text and proper support for multiple values in one frame, but some older players and devices do not read it well.

•[[[strong:ID3v1]]] - An obsolete format stored in the last 128 bytes of the file. Fields are fixed at around 30 characters, text is usually limited to ISO-8859-1 (Latin) characters, and there is no cover art.
•[[[strong:Custom fields:]]] Stored in user defined text frames (TXXX).
•[[[strong:Cover art:]]] Stored in an attached picture frame (APIC), along with its MIME type and a picture type such as front cover or back cover. A file can hold several pictures.
[[[warning:Note:]]] A file can carry both ID3v1 and ID3v2 tags at once, and different players may read different ones.
[[[italics:Key=value based]]] - Used by FLAC, Ogg Vorbis and Opus files.

Each tag is a text pair written as [[[strong:KEY=value]]], for example TITLE=Example Song. FLAC stores them in its own comment block, Ogg Vorbis in its second header packet, and Opus in a header called OpusTags.
•[[[strong:Keys:]]] Plain ASCII characters, and not case sensitive, so artist and ARTIST are the same field.
•[[[strong:Values:]]] UTF-8, so they can hold text in any language.
•[[[strong:Field names:]]] There is no fixed list, so you can add your own custom keys. A few common names (TITLE, ARTIST, ALBUM, GENRE, DATE and TRACKNUMBER) are widely used.
•[[[strong:Multiple values:]]] The same key can appear more than once, so a track with two artists simply has two ARTIST entries.
•[[[strong:Cover art:]]] FLAC has a dedicated picture block. Ogg Vorbis and Opus store the same picture data as base64 text inside a comment called METADATA_BLOCK_PICTURE.

[[[warning:Note:]]] Large embedded images in [[[strong:Ogg Vorbis]]] and [[[strong:Opus]]] files can cause problems for some older hardware players, as the picture is stored inside the comment header.
[[[italics:Atom based]]] - Used by M4A files (AAC and ALAC).
Tags are stored in atoms, which are labelled blocks inside the MP4 structure. The tags sit together in a list atom (ilst) within the file's metadata.
•[[[strong:Atom names:]]] Four-character codes, many of which begin with a © symbol, such as ©nam for the title.
•[[[strong:Numbers:]]] Track and disc numbers (trkn and disk) are stored as numbers rather than plain text.
•[[[strong:Genre:]]] ©gen holds a custom genre as text, while gnre holds a standard genre from a fixed list.
•[[[strong:Custom fields:]]] Stored in freeform atoms (----), which have their own name and an identifier such as com.apple.iTunes. Support for them varies between players.
•[[[strong:Cover art:]]] Stored in the covr atom.
[[[italics:Chunk based]]] - Used by WAV files.
Tags are stored in a LIST chunk of the type INFO. Each field is a four-character ID followed by its text.
•[[[strong:Fields:]]] A small, fixed set, such as INAM for the title, IART for the artist and IPRD for the album.
•[[[strong:Track number:]]] ITRK is widely used but is not part of the original specification, so not every program reads it.

•[[[strong:Text encoding:]]] The specification defaults to ISO-8859-1, with an optional CSET chunk to name a code page, but programs do not always follow it, so non-English characters may display incorrectly.
•[[[strong:Cover art:]]] There is no standard way to store it.
[[[warning:Note:]]] Some tools embed an ID3v2 tag inside the WAV file instead, which allows richer tags, but support for this varies between players.
[[[warning:Note:]]] When converting between formats, common fields such as the title, artist and album normally carry over, but custom fields and unusual frames may be lost.
